title: A Bi-Objective Routing Framework for Hybrid Terrestrial-Satellite Quantum Networks
abstract: Hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks combine terrestrial fiber infrastructure with free-space links to enable long-distance entanglement distribution. Entanglement can be routed over different combinations of terrestrial and satellite links, resulting in paths with different entanglement generation rates (EGRs) and fidelities. Existing routing algorithms, however, typically reduce routing to a single-objective problem by optimizing either EGR or fidelity, or by optimizing one while constraining the other, and thus do not explicitly capture the trade-off between the two. In this paper, we present a bi-objective routing framework for hybrid quantum networks that jointly optimizes end-to-end EGR and fidelity. We formulate routing as a Pareto optimization problem and show that it possesses a special mathematical structure: the bottleneck nature of end-to-end EGR and the multiplicative nature of end-to-end fidelity allow the problem to be transformed into a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem. This transformation enables the exact polynomial-time computation of a minimal complete Pareto set using Martins' bicriterion routing algorithm. Our results demonstrate that hybrid networks expose substantially richer Pareto frontiers than terrestrial-only networks and that the proposed framework outperforms representative single-objective routing policies by allowing applications to select paths based on their EGR and fidelity requirements.
summary: This paper develops a bi-objective routing framework for quantum networks combining terrestrial fiber and satellite links. It formulates the path selection as a Pareto optimization problem, jointly optimizing both entanglement generation rate and fidelity. The resulting framework allows network controllers to select the optimal path based on the specific trade-off required by the end application.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of existing quantum network routing algorithms that optimize only a single metric, proposing a framework to jointly optimize both End-to-End Entanglement Generation Rate (EGR) and fidelity.
main_result: The proposed bi-objective framework successfully models the trade-off, showing that hybrid terrestrial-satellite networks yield substantially richer Pareto frontiers than terrestrial-only links, allowing applications to select paths based on specific utility requirements.
method: The problem is formulated as a Pareto optimization problem and mathematically transformed into a MAXMIN–MINSUM bicriterion path problem, enabling the exact polynomial-time computation of the minimal complete Pareto set using Martins' bicriterion routing algorithm.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid quantum network combining static terrestrial fiber links with time-varying virtual links provided by Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. Entanglement is distributed across these mixed links.
key_observables: End-to-End Entanglement Generation Rate (EGR) and the fidelity of the distributed entanglement.
important_parameters: The network structure includes terrestrial links (limited by attenuation) and satellite links (time-varying visibility). Performance is evaluated across 24 hours.
main_assumptions: Terrestrial nodes are assumed to have perfect quantum memories, and the satellite layer assumes a dual downlink architecture without inter-satellite links.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the trade-off between EGR and fidelity for different routing policies (Pareto vs. single-objective), and one figure compares the aggregate utility (e.g., Negativity, SKR) achieved by various policies.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the bi-objective problem, models the hybrid network using time-varying graphs, derives the MAXMIN-MINSUM transformation, and then applies Martins' algorithm to compute the Pareto set, concluding with performance comparisons against single-objective baselines.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical formulation of multi-objective optimization (Pareto front) applied to quantum communication channels is highly relevant for designing robust quantum network protocols.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Trade-off between end-to-end entanglement gen- eration rate (EGR) and fidelity for routing between representative end users in Iselin, NJ and Chicago Ridge, IL. Each point represents a feasible route, while the dashed line highlights the rate-fidelity trade-off.

Fig. 2: Example of terrestrial-only and hybrid routes between Cleveland Heights, OH and High Point, NC. The green route uses only terrestrial fiber links, whereas the blue route incorporates a satellite-assisted virtual edge (dashed) between two OGSs.

Fig. 3: Simulated hybrid quantum network topology over the United States. The network integrates 1000 fiber end-nodes at the top population centers with 10 strate- gically selected Optical Ground Stations (OGS). Solid lines (green and gray) represent static terrestrial edges, while dashed lines (blue) indicate satellite-assisted vir- tual edges for a network snapshot.
Fig. 4: Selection of (a) the repeater spacing drep, and (b) the terrestrial-satellite switching distance dswitch used in the baseline distance-based routing.

Fig. 5: Temporal characteristics of the satellite-assisted virtual edge set Es(t) over a 24-hour period. Daytime solar background noise reduces the average fidelity of satellite-assisted virtual links, whereas nighttime condi- tions provide consistently higher-quality links.
